theme: Doctrinal Pause: Spiritual Gifts and the Body of Christ
doctrine: Spiritual Gifts and the Body of Christ
summary: The Spirit gives gifts for the common good; diverse members, one body; gifts ordered by love
readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 12:1-31, Romans 12:3-8, and Ephesians 4:11-16. Today is a doctrinal pause on spiritual gifts and the body of Christ. Notice who gives the gifts, what they are for, and how they work together.
settingTheScene: Three letters, three lists, one body. Paul wrote to Corinth, to Rome, and to Ephesus, each time teaching that every believer has a place in the body of Christ. Today we step back from the details of Corinth to see the overall teaching on gifts. This is also an area where evangelical Christians hold different views, especially about miraculous gifts, so it is important to learn the basics and to treat each other kindly.
observation: “Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:4).
“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7).
“All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11).
“The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you” (1 Corinthians 12:21).
“Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think” (Romans 12:3).
“Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them” (Romans 12:6).
“To equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12).
“Makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love” (Ephesians 4:16).
doctrinalFocus:
A spiritual gift is a capacity given by the Holy Spirit to a believer for serving others and building up the church. The Greek word is charisma, from charis (grace): a gift of grace. Three truths hold throughout the New Testament. First, gifts are given by the Spirit, not earned. “He apportions to each one individually as he wills.” Second, every believer has at least one gift: “To each is given.” No one is without a role. Third, gifts are for the common good, not personal status. They are tools for service, not trophies.

The lists in the New Testament are not exhaustive. 1 Corinthians 12 includes wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues, and interpretation. Romans 12 adds serving, teaching, exhorting, giving, leading, and mercy. Ephesians 4 names gifted people given to the church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, and teachers. 1 Peter 4 divides them into speaking and serving gifts. We see that gifts are as varied as the needs of the body.

Christians disagree about some gifts. Continuationists hold that all gifts, including prophecy, healing, and tongues, continue today. Cessationists hold that the miraculous sign gifts and the foundational office of apostle ceased when the New Testament was completed. Others take a position between them, expecting God to work miraculously while being cautious about claims. All agree that the Spirit is active today, that Scripture is the final authority and is complete, that gifts must be tested by the word, and that love is greater than any gift.

The body image is the center of the doctrine. A body has many parts, each necessary, none self-sufficient. The weaker parts are indispensable. The purpose is edification: “to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,” until we all attain to the unity of the faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood. Pastors and teachers are not to do all the ministry; they equip the saints to do it. The result is a church that grows “in love.”
interpretation:
In 1 Corinthians 12, the foundation is the Trinity: the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God. Diversity springs from unity. Next, purpose: “for the common good.” A gift that is not shared has missed its purpose. Third, Paul addresses two opposite attitudes. Pride says, “I do not need you.” Inferiority says, “I do not belong.” Both are corrected by the body image. If the whole body were an eye, where would be the hearing? God arranged the members as he chose.

Romans 12:3 brings humility: “By the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned.” We have received our gifts; we do not deserve them. Then the diversity: prophecy “in proportion to our faith,” service, teaching, exhortation, giving “with generosity,” leading “with zeal,” mercy “with cheerfulness.” Each gift is paired with a way of using it well.

Ephesians 4 shows how Christ is the source: “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.” Christ gave to the church leaders who equip. “Until we all attain to the unity of the faith… so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine.” Instead, “speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.”

If you are a believer, you have a gift. Find it by serving in your local church, asking others where they see God’s work through you, and trying things. Do not wait for a certainty. You cannot fully know your gift until you use it. And remember the chapter that follows 1 Corinthians 12: without love, even the best gift is nothing.
connection: Acts 6:1-7 shows the church appointing servants. Exodus 31:1-6 speaks of Bezalel being filled with the Spirit for craftsmanship. 1 Peter 4:10-11 speaks of being good stewards of God’s varied grace. Psalm 68:18 is quoted in Ephesians 4:8. Colossians 2:19 speaks of the whole body knit together. 1 Thessalonians 5:19-22 says to test everything. 1 Corinthians 14:1-5 compares tongues and prophecy. Hebrews 2:4 mentions gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will. Matthew 25:14-30 is the parable of the talents.
application:
Write down the ways you serve your local church now. If you have none, pick one place to start.

Ask two people who know you what they see as your strength in serving others.

Thank someone whose gifts are different from yours.
prayerPrompts: Thank the Holy Spirit for gifts given to every believer.
Ask him to show you what you have been given and how to use it.
Ask him to help you honor others’ gifts.
